title: How one 64-character code proves your download is real
description:
A download page lists a SHA-256 fingerprint: 64 characters, 256 bits. Run the same function on your copy and compare. A simple sum of the bytes wouldn't do: swap two bytes and the sum stays the same. SHA-256 stirs the file through 64 rounds, so flipping a single bit changes about half of the 256 output bits. There are more possible files than fingerprints, so files with the same fingerprint must exist, but finding any matching pair takes about 2^128 tries: with 8 billion people each running a billion tries a second, over a trillion years. Nobody has ever published a collision for full SHA-256.

Numbers checked in code: 100,000 one-bit flips (average 128.0 of 256 bits changed), the byte-swap example, and the 2^128 arithmetic. Sources: Wikipedia, SHA-2 (64 rounds; no attack on the full function) and Birthday attack (about 4.0×10^38 hashes for a 50% chance at 256 bits).

facts_checked: SHA-256 output: 256 bits = 64 hex characters (verify.py, hashlib)
Byte sum is unchanged when two bytes swap: 'PAY ALICE 100 EUR, PAY BOB 900 EUR' -> 'PAY ALICE 900 ..., BOB 100 ...' same sum, different SHA-256 (verify.py)
SHA-256 has 64 rounds; 'none of the attacks extend to the full round hash function' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2)

Flipping one input bit changes about half the output bits: 100,000 simulated flips, average 128.01 of 256 (verify.py); Wikipedia's SHA-224 example: 111 of 224 bits (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2)
Files of 33 bytes already outnumber 2^256 fingerprints, so collisions must exist (pigeonhole, verify.py)
Collision search ~2^128 = 3.4e38 tries; 50% chance after 4.0e38 for 256 bits (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_attack; verify.py)
8 billion people x 1e9 tries/s: 2^128 tries -> 1.35e12 years, 50% -> 1.59e12 years: over a trillion years (verify.py)

beats.say: Every file has a fingerprint twin. Nobody's ever found one.
The twins are guaranteed. Finding one is the part nobody can do.
Your four-gigabyte download: broken, or swapped by someone? You can't compare 4 billion bytes.
So compare fingerprints. The site lists one: 64 characters. Run the same recipe on your copy. Match means same file.
Don't just add up the bytes. Swap two, and the sum doesn't move. Alice 100, Bob 900 becomes Alice 900, Bob 100, and passes.
Use SHA-256. It stirs your file through 64 rounds. Change one bit, and about half of the 256 output bits flip.
But 256 bits is a finite list, and files never run out. So twins must exist. Why can't an attacker make one?
To find any matching pair, you'd hash about 2 to the 128 files. That's 340 trillion trillion trillion.
Give all 8 billion people a computer doing a billion a second. Over a trillion years.
The twin exists. It's just a trillion years away. So a matching fingerprint means you got the exact file the site published.
